newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Meridor says budget tries not to hit poor.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Meridor says budget tries not to hit poor.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor on Tuesday said efforts were made not to hurt lower-income groups in the 1997 budget but the spending package is expected to face an unusually vigorous debate in parliament.

"In this budget we made a major effort not to hurt ordinary people," Meridor told a news briefing before presenting the budget to parliament. "If there is an economic crisis, who will be out of work? The weakest classes," he said.

Meridor told parliament that the key to helping the disadvantaged was to bring Israel's economy back to a five-to-six percent annual growth rate after a sharp slowing this year in the face of widening deficits in the budget and balance of payments current account.
"These problems are likely to worsen the economic situation and the faster we solve them -- by necessary and difficult mechanisms -- the lower the cost of the correction will be," he told parliament.

Meridor faces unusally wide opposition inside his own Likud party-led coalition, most of it on the grounds that the brunt of the budget's 4.9 billion shekels ($1.5 billion) in spending cuts will hurt lower-income groups.
On Monday, virtually all the coalition parties, including some segments of the Likud, threatened to vote against the budget in the first of the three readings required before becoming law.
In past years, the budget's first reading had been passed by parliament without opposition.

In a bid to demonstrate its commitment to helping the disadvantaged, the government said it would introduce longer school days in selected parts of the country -- mainly in outlying towns populated by lower-income families.
The trial programme, which is supposed to help people by improving education and thus job prospects, will begin in January and will be financed from cuts elsewhere.

Meridor expressed confidence the budget would nevertheless pass the first reading. "It is a crucial test of responsibility for the coalition, for the government and for the Knesset (parliament) to pass this budget," he said.
The 1997 budget package calls for 190.8 billion shekels in spending and aims to keep the deficit to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Meridor refused to commit himself to further spending cuts next year but sounded optimistic that there may be no need.

"If it becomes clear that the deficit will be more than forecasted, there will be (an additional) cut," he said. But, he noted, revenues had come in slightly better than projected in September and October.
The 1997 budget is based on forecasted economic growth of 4.0 percent next year, but critics say the growth projections are too optimsitic. ($=3.26 shekels)
